title: Why an Empty List Counts as False (and What None Really Means)
excerpt: Stop 'if not score' from treating 0 as missing: learn what Python counts as False and how None differs from zero and empty values.
html:
You have probably seen code like if items: and wondered what exactly is being tested. An if runs its indented code only when its condition is true, yet here there is no comparison, no == (which asks "are these two values equal?"), just the name of a list. Python is asking a different question: is there anything in it?

Every Python value can be used as a condition: zero, empty and "nothing" values count as False, and everything else counts as True. Programmers call values that count as true "truthy" and values that count as false "falsy". This lesson maps out which is which, then looks at None, the value that means "no value at all".

Every Value Can Be Tested

Let's ask Python about a mix of values. The loop below repeats the same line for each value in the list. A quick key to the unusual ones: [] is an empty list, {} an empty dictionary, () an empty tuple and "" empty text. The function repr() shows a value with its quotes, so you can see empty and space-only text, and bool() reports whether a value counts as True or False:

values = [0, 1, -1, 0.0, "", "a", " ", [], [0], {}, (), None]

for value in values:
    print(repr(value), bool(value))
0 False
1 True
-1 True
0.0 False
'' False
'a' True
' ' True
[] False
[0] True
{} False
() False
None False

The pattern is: the number zero, the empty string, the empty list, the empty dictionary, the empty tuple and None are all False. Everything else is True.

Why is [0] true when 0 is false? Because the list is not empty: it contains one item, and the truthiness of a list depends on whether it has items, not on what they are. In the same way, a string holding a single space is True because it has a character in it.

Using Truthiness in if Statements

This is why you can write short, readable checks. An if runs the first block when its condition is true and the else block when it is not, and the method append adds an item to the end of a list:

items = []

if items:
    print("There are items to process")
else:
    print("Nothing to process")

items.append("pen")

if items:
    print("There are items to process")
else:
    print("Nothing to process")
Nothing to process
There are items to process

Wouldn't if len(items) > 0 (where len counts the items) be clearer to a beginner? It works too, and either style is fine. Most Python code uses the short form, so you will see it everywhere.

None Means "No Value"

None is a special value that stands for the absence of a value. A function (a reusable, named block of code) that never hands back a result gives None, and you can use it yourself as a placeholder for "not known yet":

result = None
print(result)
print(type(result))
print(bool(result))
None
<class 'NoneType'>
False

Isn't None just another way to write zero? No, and the difference matters. Zero is a number you can add to other numbers. None is the lack of a number:

print(None == 0)
print(None == "")
print(0 == "")
False
False
False

None is not equal to zero and not equal to the empty string, and those two are not equal to each other either. They are all "false-like" when used as a condition, but they are different values.

Test for None With is

To ask "is this value None?", write is None. Why not just compare with ==, or use the shortcut if not score? Because the shortcut cannot tell None from a real zero, as the next examples show. The word is asks "is this exactly that value?":

score = None
print(score is None)

score = 0
print(score is None)
True
False

This is the check to reach for whenever None and a valid zero or empty value could both appear. Here is the bug that the shortcut if not score creates (the word not flips true and false):

score = 0

if not score:
    print("No score yet")

if score is None:
    print("No score yet (checked with is None)")
else:
    print("The score is", score)
No score yet
The score is 0

A score of zero is a real score, yet the first check reports "No score yet" because zero is falsy. The second check asks the precise question and gets the right answer.

Get the Code

Every example in this lesson, with its output, is in a notebook on GitHub: PythonTruthinessNone.ipynb.

Summary

  • Zero, empty strings, empty lists, tuples and dictionaries, and None count as False; everything else counts as True.
  • A container's truthiness depends on whether it is empty, not on what is inside it.
  • if items: is the usual short way to ask "is there anything in it?".
  • None means "no value" and is not equal to zero or the empty string.
  • Use is None when you must tell a missing value apart from zero or empty.
